summary: This RFC outlines a plan and schedule for introducing domain-style names across the DDN and ARPA Internet. It warns that the change would affect every host. It is a planning document that preceded the real Domain Name System specifications.

plainLanguage.summary: Everyone's address was going to change to a new naming style. This note says who needs to do what and when, so nobody gets lost.

subtitle: The 1983 plan and dated schedule for moving the ARPA Internet from one host table to domain style names.

tldr.problem: Every host on the DDN/ARPA Internet relied on a single master host table, which could not keep up as hosts were added. Introducing domain style names meant changing a great deal of software.
tldr.mechanism: The plan first adds a domain style name such as USC-ISIF.ARPA to the host table, then moves translation to domain servers and resolvers, and sets requirements for new domains. A dated schedule runs from October 1983 to October 1984.
tldr.outcome: RFC 881 is a plan, not a protocol; the server and resolver design is in RFCs 882 and 883. It is updated by RFC 897.

facts.label: Servers per domain
facts.value: at least two independent (one way to meet the requirement)

today: RFC 881 is a 1983 transition plan. It is updated by RFC 897, and the domain server and resolver design it points to is in RFC 882 and RFC 883.

sections.title: Why Domain Style Names
sections.content:
Domain style names let authority and responsibility for adding hosts be delegated in a controlled way, and they split up the job of keeping host information. The split follows administrative or organizational boundaries, not necessarily network boundaries. Initially all hosts are in the domain ARPA; a second domain, DDN, comes as soon as practical, and others may follow if the requirements are met.

In the long run, special domain servers translate names to addresses. They also map mailbox addresses to the host name of a mail server, so a mailbox can belong to an organization rather than one host. The plan is carried out first in the ARPA community; the DDN Program Management Office (DDN-PMO) then sets the schedule for the DDN community.

The RFC calls the central difficulty a Catch 22: lots of software must change, some groups want domain names now and others not for a long time. Its way out is a schedule for experimenting and then authorizing use, so that anyone ready on schedule has no problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one person keeping everybody's address, each group will keep its own list. Everyone has to get ready first, so there is a calendar to follow.

sections.title: From Host Table to Servers
sections.content:
Nearly all hosts used a host table based on the master file HOSTS.TXT, kept by the Network Information Center (NIC). Step one adds a domain style name as the first name in each entry, so the entry for USC-ISIF becomes USC-ISIF.ARPA,USC-ISIF,ISIF. The RFC warns of two risks: with over five hundred entries, adding 500 names could exceed the table space in some programs, and a period is not currently a legal character in host names, so some programs may fail to parse the new names.

The domain style table is made available in parallel with the regular table for a few months and then replaces it. No new domains are added before that conversion.

Next, programs move to domain servers. A host stops holding a complete table and asks a server each time a name needs translating. The code that does this is called a resolver, and it may cache recent answers. Many hosts can swap the resolver in behind their existing name lookup function. The details are in RFC 882 and RFC 883. Eventually the master table shrinks to just the entries for the servers of the top level domains.
sections.plainLanguage: First everyone's name gets a new ending, like adding a family name. Later, instead of carrying the whole phone book, you ask a helper who knows the answer.

sections.title: Requirements on a Domain
sections.content:
To become a domain, an organization must be responsibly managed and meet four requirements.

  • Responsible person: someone with authority over names in the domain, who answers for how its hosts behave toward outside hosts and can act when one misbehaves.
  • Domain servers: a robust service, for example at least two independent servers on separate machines with no common point of failure. Sub-domains can keep the data manageable when it changes quickly.
  • Minimum size: measured by, for example, the number of hosts, the number of people with primary mailboxes, or traffic crossing the domain boundary. Specific thresholds are to be set before new domains are authorized. Being above the minimum does not force a domain to form.
  • Registration: the administrator registers with the central authority, which must be satisfied the requirements are met, and ensures host and sub-domain names conform to the naming conventions and are unique within the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: To run your own list, you need a grown-up in charge, a backup in case one helper is sick, enough people to be worth it, and to sign up with the main office.

sections.title: Mailboxes and the Two Communities
sections.content:
The domain servers support mail in two ways. Agent binding maps the right-hand part of a mailbox (the Y in X@Y) to a host that accepts the mail or forwards it, so an organization BLAT with hosts BLAT-20 and BLAT-VAX could use user@BLAT.ARPA. Mailbox binding maps the whole mailbox to a destination, which allows aliases and mailing groups but needs per-mailbox data in the server database.

The ARPA community adopts the full domain system first. The DDN community adopts domain style names but keeps a centrally maintained table copied by each host, until the DDN-PMO sets a schedule. This may mean a year or more of two schemes. The NIC will keep a HOSTS.TXT style table with names like USC-ISIA.DDN, and a domain server will hold data for the DDN domain.

The catch: that table may lack some ARPA hosts, and a DDN user replying to mail from such a host may be told there is no such host.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail can be addressed to a company instead of one computer. Meanwhile one group changes sooner than the other, so for a while some replies might not find their way.

sections.title: The Schedule
sections.content:
The schedule runs from 04-Oct-83 (the ARPANET/MILNET logical split) through 03-Oct-84, when the DDN-PMO schedules DDN implementation. Documents RFC 881, RFC 882 and RFC 883 are due 02-Nov-83, a domain style host table, DHOSTS.TXT, on 16-Nov-83, and the simple query and reply protocol and limited servers and resolvers on 15-Dec-83.

On 07-Mar-84 the domain table replaces the main host table, 02-May-84 adds the DDN domain and starts a top-level-domains-only table, DOMAINS.TXT, and 06-Jun-84 permits new domains. Full servers and resolvers, with database update support, are due 18-Jul-84, and on 05-Sep-84 the full host table for the ARPA community is discontinued.
sections.plainLanguage: The calendar lists each step, from handing out the instructions to the day the old giant list is retired.
